title: Starbursting sculptor galaxy
caption: The Sculptor Galaxy NGC 253, imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
celestial: NGC 253, Sculptor Galaxy · constellation Sculptor · about 13 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/IDA/Danish 1.5 m/ R. Gendler, U. G. Jørgensen, J. Skottfelt, K. Harpsøe

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Purple light in this picture of NGC 253 comes from an intense burst of star formation, while a yellowish colour marks dust lit up by young, massive stars. NGC 253, also called the Sculptor Galaxy, is the brightest member of the Sculptor Group. It lies about 13 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Sculptor.

It is known as a starburst galaxy because it is currently forming stars at a high rate. The frenzy of star birth began around 30 million years ago and is still going on, and the purple light traces that activity.

One result is the galaxy's superwind, a stream of energetic material pouring out from its centre into space. The image was made with the 1.5-metre Danish telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (30.17 x 15.79 arcminutes) and distance (13 million light years), the frame spans roughly 114,000 × 60,000 light-years. Its light set out about 13 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This combines visible-light observations through B, V and R filters from the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla. The source links the purple light to star formation and the yellowish colour to dust lit by young stars, but doesn't give the colour for each filter.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures collect much more light than the eye, so the faint colours of star-forming regions and dust show far more strongly.
